interviewQuestions.question: When would you fine-tune a BERT-style model instead of just calling an LLM API?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd start from the shape of the task: if it's a fixed-input, fixed-output-space understanding task — classification into known categories, NER, extractive QA — and I have a reasonable amount of labeled data (even a few thousand examples), fine-tuning a small encoder-only model is usually the better call. Three concrete reasons: cost, a fine-tuned BERT-class model at inference is orders of magnitude cheaper per request than an LLM API call; latency, encoder-only inference is a single forward pass with no autoregressive decoding loop, so it's much faster, which matters for anything real-time; and control, a fine-tuned classifier gives deterministic, well-calibrated outputs over a fixed label set, whereas prompting an LLM for classification means parsing free-form text and handling occasional format drift. The trade-off I'd flag: this only pays off if I actually have labeled data and a stable task definition — for a task that changes frequently, has no labeled data, or needs open-ended reasoning or generation, a prompted LLM is faster to stand up and more flexible. Concretely: I'd fine-tune BERT for a support-ticket classifier with 20 fixed categories and 5,000 labeled tickets, but I'd reach for an LLM for an open-ended customer-response generator.

**Testing:** whether you can reason about the cost/latency/data trade-off concretely rather than defaulting to "just use an LLM for everything", which is the wrong instinct on a fixed-classification task at scale.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Fine-tuned encoder vs prompted LLM

interviewQuestions.question: How does BERT produce a different vector for the same word 'bank' depending on whether it appears in 'river bank' or 'bank loan'?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
The token "bank" enters BERT as the exact same input embedding regardless of context — the differentiation happens entirely inside the self-attention layers, not before them. Once the sequence enters the Transformer, self-attention lets "bank"'s representation at each layer be recomputed as a weighted blend of every other token's value vector in that specific sentence, with the weights determined by how strongly "bank"'s query matches each other token's key. In "river bank," the query for "bank" ends up strongly attending to "river"'s key, pulling "river"'s value heavily into "bank"'s updated representation. In "bank loan," the same starting embedding for "bank" instead attends strongly to "loan," pulling a completely different value into its updated representation. By the time the token passes through several stacked layers of this process, its final vector has been shaped by genuinely different neighboring context in each sentence — even though the starting point (the input embedding) was identical.

This is precisely what "contextual" means as opposed to "static" embeddings like word2vec, where "bank" would map to exactly one fixed vector no matter the sentence, forcing that single vector to somehow represent an average of all of "bank"'s senses — a genuine limitation for any downstream task sensitive to which sense is meant. BERT's bidirectional pretraining objective (masked language modeling, predicting a masked word from context on both sides) is specifically what forces the model to learn to use surrounding context this way, since predicting the masked word correctly requires genuinely attending to the words around it, not just memorizing a fixed per-word mapping.

**Testing:** whether you can explain the actual mechanism (attention re-weighting per context) rather than just asserting that BERT embeddings are contextual as a fact to recite.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: How BERT actually produces context-dependent vectors

interviewQuestions.question: Why can't BERT be used directly for open-ended text generation the way GPT can?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
The blocker is architectural, not a training choice that could be easily changed after the fact. BERT is trained with fully bidirectional attention — every token attends to every other token in the input, both earlier and later — which is exactly what makes it good at understanding a complete, fixed input (predicting a masked word requires looking both left and right at real, already-present tokens). But that same bidirectionality makes it structurally unsuited for autoregressive generation: at generation time, you produce text one token at a time, and each new token can only be conditioned on tokens that already exist — there's no way to "attend to the future" for a token that hasn't been generated yet, because it doesn't exist. Feeding BERT's bidirectional attention pattern into a generation loop would require attending to tokens that are still unknown, which is a contradiction, not just a limitation.

GPT's decoder-only architecture solves this by using causal (masked) attention during training itself — every position is trained to attend only to itself and earlier positions, never later ones. This exactly matches what's actually available at generation time, so the model that was trained is directly usable for the generation process token by token, with no mismatch between training-time and generation-time information availability. BERT was never trained under that constraint, so there's no way to repurpose its trained weights for autoregressive generation without fundamentally retraining under a causal masking scheme — at which point it's no longer meaningfully "BERT," it's closer to a GPT-style decoder.

**Testing:** whether you understand the training-time/inference-time information mismatch as the actual reason, not just "BERT is for understanding, GPT is for generation" as an unexplained fact.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Why BERT can't generate text like GPT
